title: Interrupts & concurrency in Embedded C
relevance: Embedded and systems interviews probe whether candidates understand hardware preemption, why shared state between ISRs and main races, and how to keep ISRs short without inventing false atomicity.

phases.goal: Establish what a hardware interrupt does, how an ISR is entered, and the non-negotiable ISR design rules.

must_hit.point: An interrupt asynchronously preempts current CPU execution to run a dedicated Interrupt Service Routine (ISR).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says hardware asserts an IRQ, the CPU pauses the current work, and jumps to an ISR—not a normal function call from main.

must_hit.point: On IRQ, the CPU finishes the current instruction, saves state (registers and PC) to the stack, looks up the ISR address in the vector table, runs the ISR, restores context, and resumes the exact next instruction in main.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They mention context save/restore plus vector-table lookup as the hardware path into the ISR.

must_hit.point: Interrupt latency is the time from the physical event asserting the IRQ to the first instruction inside the ISR; minimizing it matters for real-time systems.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They define latency as IRQ-assert to first ISR instruction, not merely 'how long the ISR runs'.

must_hit.point: A well-designed ISR only clears the peripheral interrupt flag, does the bare minimum immediate work (e.g. read a hardware register byte), and sets a flag or pushes to a buffer so heavy work runs in main.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They recite the three-step pattern: acknowledge, minimal capture, defer—and say keep ISRs short and non-blocking.

must_hit.point: Calling printf or malloc inside an ISR is unsafe because they are blocking and non-reentrant; if main holds a lock inside malloc when the interrupt fires, the ISR can deadlock waiting for that same lock.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They explain lock/reentrancy deadlock: ISR cannot finish while main cannot resume until the ISR finishes.

probes: Walk me through what the CPU does from the moment a peripheral asserts an IRQ until main resumes.
Why is calling malloc or printf inside an ISR a bad idea?

hints.1: Think about who calls the ISR—your code, or the hardware?
hints.2: IRQ → finish current instruction → save context → vector table → ISR → restore → resume main.
hints.3: ISRs must be short: clear flag, minimal work, defer; malloc/printf can deadlock if main already holds an internal lock.

phases.goal: Show how shared globals race under preemption and which tools actually provide atomicity, visibility, or lock-free handoff.

must_hit.point: A shared counter update like event_count++ is a read-modify-write sequence; if an interrupt tears the sequence after the read, main can overwrite the ISR's update and lose the count.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They break ++ into load, increment register, store, and describe a lost update when the ISR runs mid-sequence.

must_hit.point: volatile does not make an operation atomic; it only forces real memory reads/writes for visibility so the compiler does not keep the value cached in a register forever.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They explicitly reject 'volatile means atomic' and separate visibility from indivisibility.

must_hit.point: A critical section temporarily disables interrupts around the shared update so the full RMW completes without preemption, then re-enables interrupts.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They show disable_interrupts / event_count++ / enable_interrupts (or ARM __disable_irq) as the race fix.

must_hit.point: sig_atomic_t guarantees only simple loads and stores as a single atomic unit; ++ on it is still a multi-instruction RMW. Full atomic RMW without disabling interrupts leans on C11 stdatomic.h.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They limit sig_atomic_t to load/store and do not claim ++ is atomic just because the type is sig_atomic_t.

must_hit.point: A function is reentrant if it can be interrupted mid-execution and safely called again from an ISR; shared hidden state (statics, errno, malloc) makes it non-reentrant—pass state via pointer/stack args instead.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They define reentrancy via safe nested call from ISR and name static/global/heap as failure modes.

must_hit.point: An aligned word load or store (e.g. a 32-bit integer on a 32-bit ARM Cortex-M) is typically naturally atomic in one bus cycle, but a 64-bit operation on a 32-bit MCU uses two 32-bit instructions and can be torn; memory barriers force pending reads/writes to complete for consistent views across context boundaries.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They contrast natural word atomicity with torn wide accesses and mention fences when pipelines/cores reorder memory.

must_hit.point: A lock-free SPSC ring buffer avoids critical sections by ownership split: ISR only writes head, main only writes tail; publishing relies on a word-atomic store to a 32-bit index so observers see old or new head, never a half-written value.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They assign head to the ISR and tail to main, and state that word-atomic index stores make the design work.

must_hit.point: The buffer array need not itself be atomic if the ISR writes buffer[head] before publishing the new head, and main only reads a slot after seeing the updated head.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They describe publish-after-payload sequencing as why the data slots do not need separate atomicity.

probes: Why does volatile event_count++ still race with an ISR?
How does a single-producer/single-consumer ring buffer avoid disabling interrupts?

hints.1: Ask what machine instructions a C ++ actually becomes.
hints.2: Separate visibility (volatile), mutual exclusion (critical section), and ownership split (SPSC head/tail).
hints.3: ++ is RMW and can lose updates; volatile ≠ atomic; disable IRQs briefly or use SPSC with ISR-only head and main-only tail, writing payload before publishing head.

phases.goal: Compare polling versus interrupt-driven I/O and the latency cost of overusing critical sections.

must_hit.point: Polling busy-waits on a hardware status bit: deterministic and simple, but costs 100% CPU utilization and blocks sleeping or other work.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They describe a tight while-not-ready loop and call out full CPU burn and inability to sleep.

must_hit.point: Interrupt-driven I/O lets the CPU sleep or do background work until hardware signals readiness, cutting waste and power, but adds preemption latency and concurrency hazards.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They name lower CPU/power as the win and latency plus shared-data races as the cost.

must_hit.point: Wrapping the entire main loop in a critical section would destroy interrupt latency and defeat hardware preemption; overly long critical sections also risk missing subsequent interrupts.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They refuse whole-program IRQ disable and keep critical sections as short as the protected RMW/copy.

probes: When would you choose polling over interrupts for a peripheral?
If critical sections fix races, why not disable interrupts for all of main?

hints.1: Contrast who waits: the CPU spinning, or the hardware waking you.
hints.2: List CPU/power/determinism on one axis and latency/concurrency on the other.
hints.3: Polling is simple but 100% CPU; interrupts save power but race; critical sections must stay short or you kill latency and can miss IRQs.

phases.goal: Apply the rules to torn multi-byte reads, deferred ISR work, and a UART RX ring buffer.

must_hit.point: On an 8-bit AVR, reading a 32-bit shared tick counter takes 4 instructions, so comparing or clearing it in main without a critical section can tear; the ISR may safely be the sole writer of ++ while main still needs protected multi-instruction access.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They call out multi-instruction 32-bit access on 8-bit as the tear hazard in the ticks example.

must_hit.point: Fix by briefly disabling IRQs, copying system_ticks to a local, optionally resetting under the same critical section, re-enabling IRQs, then doing slow work outside using the local copy.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They show __disable_irq / local copy / optional clear / __enable_irq / then do_something outside.

must_hit.point: In a UART RX SPSC buffer of size BUF_SIZE 64, the ISR reads the data register (clearing the flag), computes next_head, discards on full if next_head == rx_tail, otherwise stores payload then publishes rx_head; main consumes when rx_head != rx_tail and advances rx_tail.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They walk ISR push with overflow discard and main's head!=tail consume with separate head/tail ownership.

must_hit.point: A flag set in a GPIO ISR and polled in main must be volatile so the compiler re-reads it from RAM each loop instead of optimizing the check away.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They fill in volatile bool button_pressed and explain why the main loop otherwise may never see the update.

probes: Show how you would safely read a 32-bit tick counter that an ISR increments while main checks a threshold.
What goes wrong if two ISRs both push into the same SPSC ring buffer?

hints.1: Decide what must be atomic: the ISR's ++ alone, or main's multi-byte read/clear.
hints.2: Copy under a short critical section, or keep single-writer indices in an SPSC design.
hints.3: Disable IRQs only for the local snapshot/clear; for UART use ISR-only head and main-only tail with payload-before-publish; a second producer races on head.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Polling is deterministic and simple but burns 100% CPU and prevents sleep or other work; interrupt-driven I/O frees the CPU for background work and lower power until hardware signals readiness, at the cost of preemption latency and shared-data concurrency hazards.

tradeoffs.topic: Short critical sections vs wrapping all of main
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Critical sections make RMW or multi-instruction shared accesses atomic by disabling interrupts briefly; wrapping the entire main loop (or keeping sections too long) destroys interrupt latency, defeats hardware preemption, and can cause missed interrupts.

tradeoffs.topic: Critical sections vs lock-free SPSC ownership
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Disabling interrupts protects arbitrary shared RMW but costs latency; an SPSC ring buffer with ISR-only head and main-only tail avoids critical sections when a single producer and consumer and word-atomic index stores hold, but collapses if a second producer races on head.

gotchas.trap: Assuming volatile makes ++ or other multi-instruction operations atomic.
gotchas.correction: volatile only forces memory visibility (no forever-register caching); RMW on a volatile variable can still be torn by an interrupt—use a critical section, true atomics, or ownership separation.

gotchas.trap: Calling printf or malloc inside an ISR.
gotchas.correction: They are blocking and non-reentrant; if main holds an internal lock (e.g. inside malloc) when the IRQ fires, the ISR can deadlock waiting for a lock main cannot release until the ISR finishes.
sig_atomic_t only guarantees atomic simple loads and stores; ++ remains a multi-instruction RMW—use interrupt disable or C11 stdatomic for atomic RMW.

gotchas.trap: Adding a second producer to a lock-free SPSC ring buffer.
gotchas.correction: Two ISRs (or producers) both doing RMW on the shared head race; the design requires exactly one writer of head and one writer of tail.

gotchas.trap: Assuming any width of shared variable is naturally atomic on any MCU.
gotchas.correction: Aligned word load/store (e.g. 32-bit on 32-bit Cortex-M) is typically one bus cycle, but a 64-bit value on a 32-bit MCU needs two 32-bit instructions and can leave torn half-old/half-new data; likewise multi-instruction reads of wide counters on narrow CPUs need protection.
